content: The treatment outcomes for patients with multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (MDR/RR-TB) were assessed at either 18 months or, for those who had not reached a treatment outcome by 18 months, at the end of treatment outcomes occurring before 24 months. The NeXT study evaluated a 6–9 month individualized regimen (Lzd-Bdq-Lfx-PZA-Eto/Hh/Trd) compared to standard care regimens, which included both short (9–11 months) and long (18–20 months) treatments with follow-up extending to 24 months. The intervention group had a minimum follow-up of 24 months, while a small proportion of participants in the standard care group had follow-up beyond 24 months. For consistency, data were censored at 24 months. The WHO 2022 guidelines on drug-resistant TB treatment included comparisons of various regimens. The NeXT intervention (6–9 months) was compared to the WHO short regimen (9–12 months) and the WHO long regimen (18–24 months). Follow-up periods extended to 24 months, with primary analyses conducted at 12 or 18 months depending on the study. Sensitivity analyses were performed at 12, 18, and 24 months to account for relapse and death outcomes. The BPaL regimen (bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid) was evaluated in several studies, including PRACTECAL, NIX, and ZENIX. These studies assessed different linezolid doses and durations, with follow-up periods ranging from 6 months to 24 months. The primary analysis for most comparisons was conducted at 12 or 18 months, with sensitivity analyses at 24 months. The PRACTECAL trial, which included a 6-month BPaL regimen, had a larger cohort at 72 weeks (18 months) compared to 108 weeks (24 months), improving the precision of estimates at the earlier time point. For pre-extensively drug-resistant TB (pre-XDR-TB), the BPaL regimen was compared to WHO-recommended long regimens (18–24 months) and other regimens from the NIX and ZENIX studies. The primary analysis was conducted at 72 weeks, with sensitivity analyses at 24 months. The shorter BPaL regimen demonstrated potential advantages in terms of treatment duration and outcomes. Overall, the studies aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of shorter, all-oral regimens for drug-resistant TB, with a focus on relapse, death, and treatment completion rates. The findings informed the WHO's updated guidelines, emphasizing the importance of individualized treatment approaches and robust follow-up to capture long-term outcomes.
